sentences.text: Yes, senior medical students can contribute to quality assurance (QA) in day surgery.

In a study of 59 final year medical students who followed allocated patients through all phases of the day surgery process, students followed 621 cases, representing a 14.1% sampling of day surgery cases.

Students identified problems including inappropriate patient and procedure selection, inadequate pain management, discharge, communication, and resource issues, and made recommendations such as multilingual videotapes and patient information sheets, avoidance of bilateral procedures, and improved links with local medical officers.
They also developed new guidelines and protocols, indicating an active contribution to QA.

The evidence is insufficient to say whether delayed gastric emptying (DGE) after pancreaticoduodenectomy is specifically related to pylorus preservation, because the supplied study only examines patients undergoing pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (PPPD) without a comparison to pylorus resection.
In 51 PPPD patients, DGE occurred in 6 (12%).
However, DGE was much more frequent when other postoperative complications occurred (5/15, 30%) than when they did not (1/36, 3%; P=0.002).

Thus, the passages suggest DGE in this cohort was associated with postoperative complications, but they do not include a non-pylorus-preserving comparison group to establish a link to pylorus preservation itself.

Yes, the evidence indicates a relationship between rheumatoid arthritis and periodontal disease, with self-reported RA more prevalent among patients referred for periodontal treatment. In 1,412 individuals attending the University of Queensland's School of Dentistry, the prevalence of self-reported RA was 3.95% in those referred for periodontal treatment versus 0.66% in those not referred and 1% in the general population. Among referred patients with RA, 62.5% had advanced forms of periodontal disease. The passages do not address causality; RA was determined by self-report and prescription medications, and periodontal disease by existing oral radiographs.
Yes—evidence in rats indicates endothelin-1 can aggravate acute pancreatitis by transforming edematous pancreatitis into hemorrhagic pancreatitis.
In a rat model of cerulein plus restraint water-immersion stress, acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis developed in all animals, with a pancreatic hemorrhage score of 2.4 +/- 0.2.

Pretreatment with the ETA receptor antagonist BQ123 reduced the hemorrhage score to 1.0 +/- 0.0, lowered pancreatic wet weight and serum amylase, lessened histologic alterations, and improved local pancreatic blood flow.
These findings support endothelin-1, acting via ETA receptors, as an aggravating factor in this rat pancreatitis model.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether extended aortic replacement in acute type A dissection is justifiable.

In 43 consecutive patients with acute aortic dissection, complete replacement of all dissected tissue was possible in 21 (group 1) but not in 22 (group 2) because the dissection extended beyond the aortic arch.
Early mortality was 4.7%, perioperative cerebrovascular events occurred in 7.0%, and all such events occurred in group 2 (p<0.025), while 14 of 36 surviving patients had a patent false lumen.

These data suggest worse short-term outcomes when complete replacement is not feasible, but they do not directly compare an extended-replacement strategy with a limited repair, so they do not establish justifiability.

The evidence suggests yes: in 100 asthma patients, VAS dyspnea scores during a 5-20% methacholine-induced FEV1 fall were lowest in obstructed ICS-treated patients (group II) and highest in nonobstructed ICS-naive patients (group III), with ICS-treated patients scoring lower than ICS-naive patients in both obstruction strata.

However, factor analysis loaded ICS on a separate factor from PD, which loaded with PC20, and post hoc analysis showed eosinophil counts and BHR were negatively associated with PD in ICS-treated patients but eosinophil counts were positively associated with PD in ICS-naive patients.

Thus the study shows an association between ICS treatment and reduced dyspnea perception, but it does not establish a direct effect and suggests ICS may modify the relationship between inflammation/BHR and PD.
The evidence is mixed: year of radical prostatectomy was a predictor of outcome on preoperative multivariate analysis but not on postoperative multivariate analysis.

In 6,556 patients from 7 centers who underwent surgery between 1985 and 2000, with median followup 23 months, RP year was significant on preoperative analysis (p = 0.006) but not on postoperative analysis (p = 0.130).
Patient outcome steadily improved with surgery through the mid 1990s and then appeared to level off.
Yes, half-dose contrast-enhanced three-dimensional MR angiography appears sufficient for the abdominal aorta and pelvis, based on overall image quality.
In 72 consecutive patients, half-dose versus full-dose gadolinium chelate and diluted versus original concentrations were compared, with injection rates of 1 or 0.5 mL/second.

Although SNR and CNR of the abdominal aorta and common iliac artery were significantly lower in the 0.5 mL/second groups than in the 1 mL/second groups, the differences in overall image quality across the four groups were not statistically significant.
Thus, the evidence suggests half-dose imaging can be sufficient, but it does not show equivalence for quantitative SNR/CNR at slower injection rates.
Yes—for the kinematics tested, unicompartmental knee replacement preserved normal knee kinematics.

In six human cadaver knees tested during dynamic simulated stair-climbing, tibial axial rotation did not differ significantly between the intact knee and the bicruciate-retaining unicompartmental prosthesis, whereas tricompartmental replacement significantly affected tibial axial rotation (p = 0.001).
Femoral rollback was not significantly affected by either unicompartmental or tricompartmental arthroplasty, and quadriceps tension was similar among all three conditions.
These findings support restoration of normal kinematics after unicompartmental replacement, but they are limited to this cadaveric stair-climbing model.
Yes, minilaparoscopic inguinal hernia repair is feasible, based on a retrospective series of miniTAPP repairs with no conversions and minimal complications.
In 303 patients (mean age 45 years), including 213 bilateral and 90 unilateral cases, 516 groin hernia defects were repaired.
The primary endpoint was feasibility; no conversions to laparoscopy or open anterior approach occurred, there were no major complications, and minor complications were as high as 0.3%.

Yes, a subset of women with synchronous primary endometrial and ovarian cancers have Lynch syndrome, based on 2 patients meeting Amsterdam criteria for HNPCC and 5 additional medium-risk patients with molecular findings consistent with a germline MSH2 or MLH1 mutation among 59 women with tumor blocks analyzed from a cohort of 102.
None of the low-risk patients had molecular results consistent with a germline mutation.
Thus, the passages show that Lynch syndrome accounts for some, but not all, synchronous endometrial/ovarian cancers and appears concentrated in higher-risk family-history groups.
Yes—rural residence was associated with worse neonatal outcome among very premature infants, with higher adjusted mortality than urban residence.
In infants <32 weeks gestational age admitted to all 10 NICUs in NSW/ACT (1879 rural vs 6775 urban), rural residence had an adjusted odds ratio for mortality of 1.26 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.48, p = 0.005).

The pattern was consistent across subgroups, significantly for tertiary-hospital-born and 30–31 weeks gestation infants, and regional birth data also showed a higher stillbirth rate among rural infants (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.32, p<0.001).
The evidence is mixed: pharmacist education plus counter samples altered some prescribing but not others.

In a pretest-posttest controlled study, eight medical providers at an active intervention clinic in two rural southeastern Idaho private care clinics significantly decreased COX-2 NSAID prescriptions relative to total NSAIDs, from 38.9% to 23.7% (P<0.05), while seven control providers had a nonstatistically significant decrease from 67.5% to 62% (P>0.05). However, the intervention group significantly increased focus-nonsedating antihistamines from 86.7% to 93.1% (P<0.05) and PPIs from 68.9% to 86.2% (P<0.05) as percentages of total yearly prescriptions. The control group also significantly increased focus-nonsedating antihistamines (77.9% to 98.3%, P<0.05) and PPIs (77.5% to 91.4%, P<0.05), and baseline differences led the authors to focus on within-group changes rather than between-group comparisons.
No, the evidence does not show an association between recurrent spontaneous abortion and skewed X-inactivation.

In a study comparing X-inactivation patterns across five groups, the rate of extreme skewing (90% or greater) in 357 women with recurrent spontaneous abortion was 8.6%, not statistically different from any other group except the primiparous group (1.0%, P<.01).
Within the recurrent loss group, the skewing rate was also similar between women with at least one live birth (9.9%) and those with no live births and at least three losses (5.6%, P>.05).
The evidence is mixed: VEGF expression was not associated with venous invasion, but it was associated with survival in pT3 renal cell carcinoma.
In 78 patients with pT3a/pT3b tumours grouped by renal vein or vena cava invasion, only tumour size differed significantly between the groups, not VEGF expression.
VEGF expression was significantly associated with survival on univariate analysis (p<0.01) and was an independent predictor on multivariate analysis (OR 6.07).
The available evidence does not support being small for gestational age as a risk factor for retinopathy of prematurity.

In a prospective cohort of preterm infants with birth weight ≤1,500 g and gestational age ≤32 weeks, any-stage ROP occurred in 24.7% of SGA versus 33.2% of AGA infants (p = 0.111), and severe ROP in 6.2% versus 7.5% (p = 0.779), differences that were not statistically significant.
After adjusted logistic regression, weight gain from birth to the sixth week of life and need for blood transfusions, but not SGA status, were significant risk factors for ROP.
No—the evidence indicates accurate tidal volume delivery is difficult and not reliable with a manual resuscitator.

In 114 individuals trained in basic life support and bag-valve-mask ventilation, mean tidal volumes differed significantly by squeezing method: one-handed 592.84 mL (SD 117.39), two-handed 644.24 mL (SD 144.7), and two-handed half-compression 458.31 mL (SD 120.91) (p<0.01).

Two-handed delivery produced significantly greater volume than one-handed delivery (r = 0.398, p<0.01), while physical characteristics such as hand size, volume, and grip power showed no correlation with delivered volume and education/practice had only weak correlations.

The passages show difficulty and variability in volume delivery but do not define a target tidal volume or accuracy threshold, so they do not establish that accurate delivery is impossible in all cases.

The evidence is insufficient to determine whether telmisartan prevents hepatic fibrosis in rats with alloxan-induced diabetes, because the supplied results report TGF-beta immunoreactivity and hepatocyte density but not fibrosis itself.

In 15 adult male rats, alloxan-induced diabetic rats treated with telmisartan (10 mg/kg/day orally for 30 days) showed a significant difference in numerical density of hepatocytes compared with diabetic controls, and their liver sections showed no TGF-beta immunoreactivity whereas diabetic controls were strongly immunoreactive.
These findings suggest an effect on TGF-beta expression and hepatocyte changes, but they do not provide direct evidence that telmisartan prevents hepatic fibrosis.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that preventing osteoporosis is the key to eliminating aromatase inhibitor (AI)-related musculoskeletal symptoms, because the study only found an association between bone mineral density (BMD) and symptoms, not causation.

In a retrospective chart review of 316 patients with hormone receptor-positive nonmetastatic breast cancer on AIs for at least 3 months with DEXA, musculoskeletal symptoms were significantly associated with DEXA-BMD (P<.001), and patients receiving AIs plus calcium/bisphosphonate had more patients without musculoskeletal symptoms and fewer fractures.
The study also found that prior tamoxifen and steroidal versus nonsteroidal AIs were associated with symptom and fracture differences (P<.001).
However, it did not test whether preventing osteoporosis eliminates symptoms, and the mechanism and risk factors remain poorly studied.
No—routine intensive or invasive investigation may not be necessary in all cases of cholestasis associated with small bowel atresia.

In a retrospective review of 53 patients with SBA, 24 (45%) developed postoperative cholestasis, but no patient had biliary atresia, no deaths were related to isolated cholestasis/cirrhosis, and cholestasis resolved spontaneously in all survivors.

Ten patients (36%) underwent in-depth evaluations and 8 (28%) had liver biopsy, which the authors suggest may be unnecessary when cholestasis is attributed to prolonged parenteral nutrition or delayed enteral feeding.
The passage does not provide explicit guidelines, but it indicates that investigation is not always warranted.
No; a cross-sectional study in an ethnically diverse urban population found no association between obesity or increasing BMI and asthma control.

In 292 adults with asthma (mean age 47 years, 82% women, 67% African American, 63% obese), regression analysis showed no association between obesity or increasing BMI and asthma control using all four validated questionnaires, even after adjusting for FEV1, smoking status, race, sex, comorbidities, and long-term controller use.
Mean scores indicated suboptimal control (ACCI 8.3/19, ACT 15.4/25, ACQ 2.1/6, ATAQ 1.3/4), but BMI was not linked to worse control.
Yes, elective re-siting of intravenous cannulae decreased peripheral thrombophlebitis in a small randomized trial of patients having major abdominal surgery.
In that trial, control cannulae were removed only for pain, dislodgement, or signs/symptoms of PVT, while study cannulae were changed and re-sited every 48 hours.
The incidence of PVT was 100% (21/21) in the control group versus 9.5% (2/21) in the study group (p<0.0001), and severity was also lower in the study group.
The evidence is mixed: responsibility appears to affect valuation for some health-care-caused harms but not consistently across all categories.

In an online survey of 1,030 people reflecting the UK population, participants used a person trade-off to compare preventive interventions of equal cost and equal health benefit per person that differed in causation.

They valued preventing hospital-acquired infections (1.31) more than genetic disorders (1.0), valued drug errors similarly (1.07), and valued injuries to health care staff less (0.71); lifestyle-related interventions (0.65) and sports injuries (0.41) were also weighted less.

Thus, in this study, health-care responsibility was associated with higher valuation only for hospital-acquired infections, while other health-care-caused harms were not valued more and some were valued less.

Yes, meta-analytic evidence indicates progressive brain changes in schizophrenia, with patients showing significantly greater longitudinal decreases in several brain volumes and greater increases in lateral ventricles than healthy controls.

In a systematic review of 27 longitudinal volumetric MRI studies including 928 patients and 867 controls, the differences in annualized percentage volume change between patients and controls were -.07% for whole brain volume, -.59% for whole brain gray matter, -.32% for frontal white matter, -.32% for parietal white matter, -.39% for temporal white matter, and +.36% for bilateral lateral ventricles.
These findings support progression over the 1- to 10-year scan intervals studied.
Yes, symptoms matter in older adults being considered for phase I clinical trials, because having more than 3 symptoms was associated with worse outcomes.

In a retrospective chart review of 56 participants older than 60 years, those with >3 symptoms had more admissions (37.5% vs 14.29%; P =.0335), more complications (46.43% vs 16.07%; P =.0026), and greater functional decline (24 vs 8; P =.0173) than those with ≤3 symptoms.
These findings suggest symptom burden should be considered when evaluating such patients for phase I trials.

Yes, some type II supracondylar humerus fractures can be treated nonoperatively; in a prospective registry of 259 pediatric type II fractures, 150 (57.9%) were ultimately treated without surgery, although 39 failed nonoperative alignment and were taken for surgery.

Nonoperative management was more likely successful in fractures without rotational deformity or coronal angulation and with a shaft-condylar angle >15 degrees, and patients with isolated extension deformity but none of the other features were more likely to complete successful nonoperative management.
At final follow-up, change in carrying angle, range of motion, and complications did not show clinically significant differences between nonoperative and surgical treatment groups.
Thus, the passages show that a subset can be managed nonoperatively, but they also indicate that determining which type II fractures will succeed without surgery is the clinical challenge.

Yes, pancreas retransplantation appears to offer a viable second chance for diabetic patients, based on second graft survival comparable to primary grafts and significantly better than their failed first grafts.

In a study of 569 pancreas transplantations including 37 second transplantations (17 from 1995), second pancreas survival was 71% at 1 year and 59% at 5 years, similar to primary graft survival in the whole population (79% and 69%; P=0.5075) and significantly better than the same patients' first graft survival (29% and 7%; P=0.0008).
Patient survival was 89% at 5 years, and pancreas retransplantation had no impact on kidney graft function or survival (100% at 5 years).

The evidence is insufficient to regard pulp chamber pulpotomy as a permanent treatment; in a small series, 24-month survival without complementary treatment was 82%, and 3 of 17 teeth required root canal treatment (two for pain control, one for prosthetic reasons).

The study included 17 patients aged 7-54 years with vital pulps and no clinical evidence of irreversible pulpitis, treated by pulpotomy with ProRoot MTA in premolar or molar teeth and followed for 12 to 24 months.
These findings show short-term success in most cases but do not establish permanence, given the need for further treatment in some teeth and the limited follow-up.

No, the evidence suggests routine delayed-phase imaging is generally not worth the additional radiation in routine abdominopelvic CT, because it benefited only 4.2% of patients and increased effective radiation dose by a mean of 59.5%.

In 1000 consecutive patients (912 men, 88 women; average age 60) undergoing routine contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT and excluding multiphasic indications, delayed phase added characterization or detection in 42 patients (4.2%), mostly incidental liver hemangiomas, adrenal adenomas, or parapelvic renal cysts that could be confirmed noninvasively.
Only one patient (0.1%) had an important finding (renal mass) seen only on delayed phase, while 958 patients (95.8%) had no benefit.
The passage does not provide time data, so the time component remains unaddressed.
The evidence is mixed: for SSI enrollees, PSNs lowered PMPM expenditures by $7 more than HMOs, but the supplied passages do not compare PSNs with primary care case management.

This rests on Florida Medicaid claims from two pre-Demonstration and four post-implementation fiscal years in two urban Demonstration and two urban non-Demonstration counties, totaling 26,819,987 person-months, analyzed with difference-in-differences.

Overall, the Demonstration produced lower PMPM expenditure increases over time among SSI enrollees ($40 vs $186 in non-Demonstration counties), and PSNs lowered PMPM expenditures by $7 more than HMOs; savings among TANF enrollees were smaller.
Thus, the passages support lower expenditures for PSNs versus HMOs among SSI enrollees, but they do not settle PSNs versus primary care case management.
Yes, pharmacologic prophylaxis for knee osteoarthritis can be cost-effective, but only in high-risk patients and at low drug costs.

In a simulation model, base-case DMOAD prophylaxis initiated at age 50 with 40% first-year efficacy, 5% annual failure, 0.22% major toxicity, and $1,000 annual cost in a high-risk cohort (obese with prior knee injury) increased QALYs by 0.04 and lifetime costs by $4,600, yielding an ICER of $118,000 per QALY gained.
For the knee injury only cohort, ICERs exceeded $150,000/QALY, and for obese only or no risk factors, prophylaxis was less cost-effective than standard of care.
Regimens priced at $3,000 per year or higher had ICERs above current US cost-effectiveness thresholds.
Yes—several factors are associated with higher staple line leak rates after primary sleeve gastrectomy for morbid obesity.

In a German registry analysis of 5,400 primary laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomies over 7 years, male gender, higher BMI, concomitant sleep apnea, conversion to laparotomy, longer operation time, use of both buttresses and oversewing, and intraoperative complications were each significantly associated with higher leakage, while the overall leak rate fell from 6.5% to 1.4%.
On multivariate analysis, however, only operation time and year of procedure had a significant independent impact on staple line leak rate.
No, resected stomach volume was not significantly related to weight loss after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy.

In 100 patients divided by resected stomach volume (700–1,200 mL, 1,200–1,700 mL, and >1,700 mL), there were no significant differences in mean percentage excess body weight loss (%EBWL) among the three groups at 3, 6, 12, or 24 months.
Overall mean %EBWL was 37.68 ± 10.97, 50.97 ± 13.59, 62.35 ± 11.31, and 67.59 ± 9.02 % at those time points, respectively.
Resected stomach volume was greater with higher preoperative BMI and positively associated with resected stomach weight, but this did not translate into differential weight loss.

No—the proposed clinical identifiers for early-stage primary/idiopathic adhesive capsulitis do not appear to reflect the real picture, based on only 25% of clinically diagnosed patients having a positive anesthetic response and the surviving identifier being associated with reduced odds of that response.

In a cross-sectional study of 64 patients diagnosed with early-stage adhesive capsulitis by a physical therapist or medical practitioner, 8 active and 8 passive shoulder movements and visual analog scale pain scores were recorded before and immediately after intra-articular corticosteroid and local anesthetic injection, with ≥70% pain relief for passive external rotation defined as a positive anesthetic response.

Only 16 participants (25%) demonstrated a positive anesthetic response, and univariate logistic regression found that global loss of passive range of movement (OR=0.26, P=.03), pain at the end of range of all measured active movements (OR=0.06, P=.02), and global loss of passive glenohumeral movements (OR=0.23, P=.02) were associated with it.

After stepwise removal, pain at the end of range of all measured active movements remained the only identifier but was associated with reduced odds of a positive anesthetic response, and the lack of a recognized reference standard for diagnosing early-stage adhesive capsulitis remains problematic.

Yes—among 244 emergency medicine residents at 9 academic medical centers, residency programs with emergency ultrasound fellowships were associated with residents reporting more ultrasound scans than programs without fellowships (P =.04).
The study also found significant differences between fellowship and non-fellowship programs in most bedside ultrasound applications and in barriers to residents' ultrasound education (P <.05).
The study design was cross-sectional, so it shows an association but does not establish causation.
The evidence is insufficient to establish scintigraphy as a guideline method for determining amputation levels in diabetic foot, because the supplied study only evaluated its potential use.

In 30 diabetic foot patients, 3-phase bone scintigraphy with technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate marked the most distal perfused site as the amputation level, alongside Doppler ultrasound and surgical inspection of an infection-free clear region.
The results report amputation levels and reamputations in seven patients but provide no guideline recommendation or comparison to a reference standard.
Yes—one randomized prospective study found that more frequent skin care reduced IAD severity in critically ill patients.

In 99 progressive care patients who were incontinent or had a diversion/catheter for more than 2 days, the intervention group received a defined skin care protocol every 6 hours and the control group every 12 hours, with both also receiving it as needed.
At discharge, the intervention group had significantly less moderate IAD (7.1%) than the control group (10.9%; P ≤ 0.001).
These passages support a frequency effect but are limited to this single study.

Yes, early extubation should generally be the goal for children after congenital cardiac surgery, though not universally (e.g., Norwood operations), based on a study showing it was feasible in most patients and associated with lower mortality and reintubation.

In 613 children, including 97 neonates, intraoperative extubation was achieved in 71% and extubation within 24 hours in 89%; early versus delayed extubation was associated with lower mortality (1% vs 9%, P<.001) and lower reintubation (4% vs 23%, P<.001).

Neonates were also frequently extubated within 24 hours (63%), including 67% after arterial switch and 54% after total anomalous pulmonary venous return repair, but no Norwood patient was extubated within the first 24 hours.

Predictors of delayed extubation included preoperative mechanical ventilation, weight <5 kg, longer procedure time, and postoperative inotrope support, while the strategy was associated with low complications (5.1 per 10 procedures) and short median ICU (1 day) and hospital (4 days) stays.
No, adding ganglionated plexi ablation to Maze IV was not beneficial for long-term stable sinus rhythm in the supplied study.

In 519 patients with persistent or long-standing persistent AF undergoing radiofrequency Maze IV, the proportion in normal sinus rhythm off antiarrhythmic drugs did not differ between those without versus with GP ablation (75.5% vs 67.8%, p=0.08) at a median follow-up of 36.7 months.

Absence of GP ablation was not a significant predictor of AF recurrence (p=0.12), while longer AF duration, larger left atrial dimensions, absence of connecting lesions, and absence of right atrial ablation were significant predictors.

The evidence is mixed: automated, at-the-visit tailored prompts about family history risk led PCPs to review or discuss family history at many visits but did not significantly change problem summary list documentation of risk status or screening interventions for any of the six diseases.

In 492 community-based primary care patients aged 35 to 65 with moderate or strong familial risk for heart disease, stroke, diabetes, or breast, colorectal, or ovarian cancer, there were 847 visits; 152 had no documentation of a response.

Of the remaining 695 visits, PCPs reviewed family history in 372 (53.5%), discussed it in 159 (22.9%), did not address it in 155 (22.3%), and reviewed it plus ordered tests/referrals in 5 (0.7%), with no significant change in problem summary list documentation or screening for any disease.
No; in this study base deficit on admission did not significantly predict mortality in patients with isolated severe traumatic brain injury.
Among 108 patients over age 16 treated from 2009 to 2013, 88 (81.5%) had base deficit and 62 (58.5%) had unfavorable outcomes.

There was no statistically significant difference in mean base deficit between survivors and non-survivors, and the area under the ROC curve for base deficit as a predictor of mortality was statistically non-significant.
No—in elderly patients undergoing aortic valve replacement with small prostheses, patient-prosthesis mismatch did not affect survival or quality of life.

Among 152 patients aged at least 75 years with pure aortic stenosis who received 19- or 21-mm valves, PPM occurred in 78 patients (53.8%), including 42 (29%) with indexed effective orifice area less than 0.75 cm²/m² and 17 (11.7%) with less than 0.65 cm²/m².
Five-year overall survival was 78 ± 4.5% and was not influenced by PPM (P = NS), while quality-of-life scores were similar to those of no-PPM patients (P = NS).
Functional status in long-term survivors with PPM improved from mean NYHA class 3.0 to 1.7 (P < 0.001).
The evidence is consistent with, but does not prove, that altered maternal creatine homeostasis during gestation in the spiny mouse is a metabolic adaptation to pregnancy.

In pregnant (n=8) versus age-matched virgin female spiny mice (n=6), plasma creatine and renal creatine excretion decreased significantly from mid to late gestation (P<0.001 and P<0.05, respectively).

At term, pregnancy increased lean tissue, kidney, liver, and heart mass (P<0.01, P<0.01, P<0.01, P<0.05), increased heart and skeletal muscle CrT1 expression (both P<0.05), increased heart and kidney creatine content (P<0.05 and P<0.001), up-regulated renal AGAT mRNA/protein (P<0.01/P<0.05), and down-regulated heart and brain AGAT/GAMT expression.
These descriptive changes support altered maternal creatine handling but do not by themselves establish that the changes are an adaptive metabolic response to pregnancy.
No—adherence was incomplete among tuberculosis patients in this Chinese cohort, with 36.0% experiencing non-adherence.

In a prospective cohort of 481 newly confirmed TB patients from three counties in western China followed from 2012 to 2013, 28.2% were lost to follow-up, and only 13.9% took drugs under direct observation while 60.5% were supervised by phone calls.
The study therefore shows substantial non-adherence in this population, but it does not by itself establish adherence levels for all TB patients across China.

Yes, overexpression of Ki-67 appears to be a prognostic biomarker of upper tract urinary carcinoma, based on an immunohistochemistry study plus meta-analysis showing high Ki-67 associated with poorer survival and disease progression.

In UTUC patients, those with muscle-invasive tumors (T2-T4) had higher Ki-67 expression than those with non-muscle-invasive tumors (Tis-T1), and high Ki-67 expression was linked to significantly poorer cancer-specific survival (CSS) and disease-free survival (DFS).

Multivariate analysis found Ki-67 an independent prognostic factor for CSS (HR=3.196) and DFS (HR=3.517), and a meta-analysis of 12 studies with 1,740 patients reported pooled hazard ratios of 2.081 for poor survival and 2.791 for disease progression, with significant subgroup HRs for CSS (2.276), metastasis-free survival (3.008), and DFS (6.336).

The evidence is mixed or insufficient to conclude that lower limb fractures should be treated surgically in patients with chronic spinal cord injuries, because one study found better outcomes with surgery but noted no consensus and a conservative trend.
In 37 lower limb fractures in patients with chronic spinal cord injuries, 25 were treated surgically and 12 orthopaedically.

Surgical patients had better clinical results, range of motion, bone consolidation, and less pressure ulcers and radiological misalignment, with no differences in pain, hospital stay, or medical complications.
However, the authors state there is no current consensus and the trend has been conservative due to high complication rates in surgical treatment.
Thus, the passages suggest possible surgical benefit but do not settle whether surgery should be used routinely.

Yes, lunar position appears to influence the time of delivery, based on a reported connection between the distribution of spontaneous full-term deliveries and the lunar month in a retrospective study of 1248 deliveries over 36 lunar months.
The effect of lunar phases was particularly relevant in multiparae and plurigravidae, where the mean day of delivery corresponded to the first or second day after the full moon.
This was a single-center retrospective analysis using circular statistics, so it supports an association in that population but does not establish causation or generalizability.

Yes—immunohistochemistry demonstrated estrogen and progesterone receptors in anal canal tissues, supporting a possible hormonal influence on anal continence, though the passages do not directly test incontinence outcomes.

In 35 anorectal specimens from 21 patients (14 women, 7 men), ER was found in internal sphincter smooth muscle of all females (10/10) and 4/7 males, and in perimuscular connective tissue of all females (12/12) and 4/7 males.
No specific ER or PR staining was seen in external sphincter striated muscle nuclei in either sex (n=8).
In females, about 50% of ER-positive tissues were also PR-positive; in males only one had PR, confined to smooth muscle.

No—in a prospective follow-up, no significant differences in rate of cognitive decline, mortality, or progression to dementia were found between subjects with and without hippocampal atrophy (HCA) on MRI.

The comparison included 5 controls with HCA and 5 without, 7 depressed subjects with HCA and 7 without, and 12 clinically diagnosed probable AD subjects with HCA and 12 without, followed at approximately 2 years with repeat cognitive testing using CAMCOG.
HCA was rated by two radiologists blind to cognitive test scores.
These findings are from small groups and do not establish that HCA has no predictive value in other populations.
No, the Child Health Computing System did not adequately identify children with cerebral palsy, as 47% of cases on the Northern Ireland Cerebral Palsy Register were not found on the CHCS.
This comparative survey included children with cerebral palsy aged 5-9 years in one Health and Social Services Board in Northern Ireland and compared CHCS records with the NICPR.
Of 135 cases recorded on the NICPR, 47% were absent from the CHCS, and most of these had no computer record of any medical diagnosis.
Among 82 cases recorded on the CHCS, 10 (12%) were not on the NICPR, and 5 (6%) were found on follow-up not to have CP.
